slides.title: HIV test (screening)
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 1/4
bullets: Specimen: Venous or finger-stick blood, oral fluid (saliva); sometimes urine — depends on the test type

What it is used for: Everyone aged 13 to 64 should be tested for HIV at least once. With risk factors — at least once a year: for example, more than one sex partner since the last test, sex with a partner who has HIV, sharing needles or injection equipment, exchanging sex for money or drugs, or a diagnosis of another sexually transmitted infection, hepatitis or tuberculosis. HIV testing is recommended during each pregnancy.

slides.title: HIV test (screening)
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 2/4
bullets: CDC advises clinicians to use an “opt-out” approach: HIV testing is included in standard preventive screening for all patients, who are told they may decline. This approach removes stigma associated with testing and fosters earlier diagnosis.

After a possible exposure, talk with a provider right away about post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): started within three days of a possible exposure, it may prevent HIV infection. HIV tests are needed during and after PEP.

slides.title: HIV test (screening)
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 3/4
bullets: Physiology: HIV destroys certain immune system cells. It spreads through contact with blood and other body fluids — usually during sex or when sharing needles or other drug-injection items. Without treatment, HIV gradually destroys the immune system and leads to AIDS, its most serious stage. Most people with HIV do not have AIDS, and taking HIV medicines as prescribed may prevent AIDS altogether.

slides.title: HIV test (screening)
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 4/4
bullets: There are three types of HIV tests: antibody tests (IgM and/or IgG antibodies), antigen/antibody tests (p24 antigen plus IgM and IgG antibodies) and nucleic acid tests (NAT, viral RNA). The p24 antigen, part of the virus itself, can be detected before antibodies develop. Antigen/antibody tests on venous blood are recommended for, and common in, laboratory testing.

slides.title: HIV test (screening)
cols: A positive result means signs of HIV were found and a follow-up test is needed to confirm the diagnosis (unless it was a NAT). In a health care setting or lab, the lab runs the follow-up test, usually on the same sample; after a positive self-test or community test, see a provider. If the follow-up test is also positive, it means HIV.

No test can detect HIV immediately after infection — this is the window period. Usual detection times: antibody tests 23–90 days after exposure; rapid finger-stick antigen/antibody test 18–90 days; lab antigen/antibody test on venous blood 18–45 days; NAT 10–33 days.

slides.title: HIV test (screening)
cols: An HIV diagnosis does not mean AIDS. Treatment should start as soon as possible: antiretroviral therapy (ART) can lower the virus in blood until a test cannot detect it, and with an undetectable viral load HIV is not transmitted through sex (“Undetectable = Untransmittable”).
After a negative result following an exposure, test again once the window period for that test type has passed.
A negative result means no signs of HIV were found, but it does not always mean there is no HIV.

slides.title: HIV test (screening)
cols: After a negative rapid or at-home test, an exposure 90 or more days ago means you can be confident; less than 90 days ago usually means another test later. The result shows only your own status, not your partner’s.

slides.title: HIV test (screening)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed. The sample is venous blood, finger-stick blood, oral fluid collected with a swab along the gums, or urine. Rapid tests give results in 30 minutes or less; a lab antigen/antibody test or NAT may take several days. With an at-home test, follow the kit instructions exactly.

slides.title: HIV test (screening)
bullets: Limitations: NAT detects HIV sooner than other tests, but because it is expensive it is mostly used to monitor treatment rather than for routine screening. With a recent possible exposure, early HIV symptoms (fever, chills, extreme fatigue, swollen lymph nodes, rash, mouth sores, night sweats and others) and a negative antibody or antigen/antibody test, a NAT should be considered.

HIV testing can be anonymous: you get a number instead of giving your name and use that number to get your results. A provider or HIV counselor can explain the result and whether another test is needed.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 1/8
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood; cerebrospinal fluid if nervous system involvement is suspected

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 2/8
bullets: What it is used for: Testing is done with symptoms of syphilis or if a sex partner was recently diagnosed. Second-stage symptoms include fever and swollen glands, a rough red rash usually on the palms or soles, headache or muscle aches, sore throat, fatigue, weight loss and patchy hair loss.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 3/8
bullets: With high risk (multiple partners, sex without a condom, HIV, another sexually transmitted disease, sex with men who have sex with men), regular testing is advised even without symptoms.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 4/8
bullets: Syphilis testing is needed in pregnancy: passing the infection to the fetus can cause serious, sometimes deadly problems. CDC recommends testing at the first prenatal visit and, with higher risk, again at 28 weeks and at delivery.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 5/8
bullets: Physiology: Syphilis tests usually look for antibodies to the bacterium that causes syphilis. The first step is screening: RPR (an antibody called reagin) or VDRL (on blood or spinal fluid, a broader range of antibodies). These antibodies are also made in some autoimmune diseases and other infections, so a positive screen is followed by a second, confirmatory test.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 6/8
bullets: The confirmatory test usually looks for antibodies the immune system makes only against syphilis (e.g., TP-PA, TPHA, FTA-ABS, enzyme or chemiluminescence immunoassays). If present, the person either has syphilis now or had syphilis that was treated. Sometimes the bacteria themselves are looked for instead, but only specialized labs can do this.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 7/8
bullets: Syphilis spreads through vaginal, oral or anal sex and can pass to a fetus during pregnancy. The first stage starts 2–12 weeks after exposure with a painless sore (chancre) that can go unnoticed; the second starts 1–6 months after the chancre heals; untreated, a latent stage lasting years follows — without symptoms the infection can still spread and cause damage; the fourth stage brings severe problems such as dementia and blindness.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 8/8
bullets: It is easiest to cure early.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: Positive result: Per CDC, a presumptive diagnosis of syphilis requires two kinds of serologic tests: a nontreponemal test (VDRL or RPR) and a treponemal test (TP-PA, various enzyme and chemiluminescence immunoassays, immunoblots or rapid treponemal assays). One type alone is insufficient. Anyone with a reactive nontreponemal test should get a treponemal test to confirm the diagnosis (traditional algorithm).

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: Positive result: Some labs use a reverse sequence: an automated treponemal immunoassay (EIA or CIA) first and, if positive, a quantitative nontreponemal test with titer. If the nontreponemal test is negative, a different treponemal test (preferably TP-PA) adjudicates. If that second treponemal test is also negative and the risk is low, no further evaluation or treatment is indicated.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: Positive result: If the follow-up test confirms syphilis, treatment is usually penicillin: antibiotics cure most early-stage infections, but in later stages cannot undo damage already done. Sex partners should be told so they can be tested and treated if needed, and screening tests are repeated to check how well treatment is working.

Negative result: A negative screening result means you probably do not have syphilis, but it does not completely rule it out: antibodies can take a couple of weeks to develop. Another test may be needed after a suspected exposure.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a blood test. If syphilis may be affecting the brain, spinal cord or nerves, cerebrospinal fluid is tested via a lumbar puncture, before which you may be asked to empty your bladder and bowels. At-home blood collection kits are screening tests only — another test is needed to confirm the diagnosis.

Interferences: False-positive nontreponemal results can occur with conditions unrelated to syphilis: other infections (e.g., HIV), autoimmune conditions, vaccinations, injection drug use, pregnancy and older age.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: Limitations: Nontreponemal titers can reflect disease activity and are used to monitor treatment; results are reported quantitatively (highest titer). A fourfold change (two dilutions, e.g., from 1:16 to 1:4) is needed for a clinically significant difference. Serial tests use the same method (VDRL or RPR), preferably in the same lab: VDRL and RPR titers cannot be compared directly, and RPR titers are often slightly higher.

Most patients with a reactive treponemal test stay reactive for life, regardless of treatment or disease activity (15%–25% of those treated in the primary stage become nonreactive after 2–3 years). Treponemal antibody titers do not predict treatment response and should not be used for that purpose.

slides.title: Syphilis tests: RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TP-PA
bullets: No single test diagnoses neurosyphilis: CSF findings (cell count, protein, CSF-VDRL), blood serology and neurologic signs are assessed together. CSF-VDRL is highly specific but insensitive; CSF FTA-ABS is less specific but highly sensitive.

In certain parts of the world, bacteria closely related to the syphilis bacterium spread through non-sexual skin contact with sores and cause yaws, bejel and pinta. Blood tests cannot tell them apart from syphilis — the provider relies on the skin sores and medical and travel history.

slides.title: A lab antigen/antibody test on venous blood is negative 14 days after a possible exposure. Correct conclusion?
options: Still in the window period — test again after the window for this test type
HIV is definitely ruled out, because a lab test detects infection earlier than a rapid test and no other test is needed
A negative result means immunity to HIV
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. 14 days is shorter than this test’s window period, so a negative result does not rule out HIV.

Basis: A lab antigen/antibody test usually detects HIV 18–45 days after exposure.

slides.title: A screening RPR is reactive. Which next step fits the source?
options: Syphilis is confirmed — treatment and partner notification without other tests are enough
The result is false: RPR is reliable only in spinal fluid
A treponemal test (e.g., TP-PA or an immunoassay)
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. A reactive nontreponemal test should always be followed by a treponemal test.

Basis: Nontreponemal tests can be reactive in other conditions; diagnosis needs two kinds of tests.

Determining CRP, RF, ASO. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 1. CRP is an acute-phase protein; immunoturbidimetry/nephelometry (quantitative) or latex agglutination (semi-quantitative); <3 mg/L normal; rises sharply in bacterial infection; hs-CRP – cardiovascular risk.

2. Rheumatoid factor (RF) – autoantibodies to the Fc portion of IgG (mainly IgM); latex agglutination or nephelometry; occurs in rheumatoid arthritis but is not specific (other rheumatic diseases, infections, healthy elderly); anti-CCP is more specific.

slides.title: Determining CRP, RF, ASO. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 3. ASO (antistreptolysin-O) – antibodies to streptolysin O of group A streptococcus; begin to rise ~1 week after infection, peak at 3–6 weeks; a sign of recent streptococcal infection (rheumatic fever, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis); dynamics in paired sera are important.
4. Disadvantages of latex tests: semi-quantitative, prozone effect, subjective reading; quantitative immunoturbidimetric methods are preferred in modern practice.
5. Results are interpreted with the clinical picture: RF/ASO alone is not a diagnosis.

slides.title: Laboratory diagnosis of allergic diseases?
bullets: 1. Distinguishing types of allergy: IgE-mediated (type I) and non-IgE-mediated reactions; laboratory tests are interpreted together with the history.
2. General laboratory signs: eosinophils in blood and in nasal smear/sputum; total IgE – nonspecific (also raised in helminthiasis), a normal value does not exclude allergy.
3. Specific IgE (in vitro immunoassay) shows sensitization to an allergen; sensitization does not always mean clinical allergy.

slides.title: Laboratory diagnosis of allergic diseases?
bullets: 4. Skin prick test: read at 15–20 minutes, a wheal ≥3 mm larger than the negative control is positive; histamine – positive control; antihistamines make the result falsely negative.
5. Additional: component-resolved diagnostics, provocation tests (under specialist supervision), tryptase in anaphylaxis; compare with clinical data in interpretation.

slides.title: TORCH infections, general description?
bullets: 1. TORCH is a group of infections dangerous to the fetus and newborn in pregnancy: Toxoplasmosis, "Other" (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19, Zika, etc.), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes simplex.

2. Most dangerous is primary infection during pregnancy (especially rubella – in the first trimester; toxoplasmosis); but 50–75% of congenital CMV occurs in mothers infected before pregnancy (reactivation/reinfection).
3. Consequences: fetal death, congenital malformations (congenital rubella syndrome), hearing loss (CMV), eye and CNS damage (toxoplasmosis, CMV), neonatal herpes.

slides.title: TORCH infections, general description?
bullets: 4. Routes of transmission: transplacental, through the birth canal, after birth (breast milk – CMV).
5. Prevention: rubella vaccination (check immunity before pregnancy), hygiene measures (CMV, toxoplasmosis), screening and targeted testing.
